definition: Bard means a poet, often a singer as well.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word bard. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know bard should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Carved over the concert hall's door is a bard with his harp, mid-verse, mouth open in stone song.
A rhymer sits far below a bard — birthday couplets and refrigerator verse, nothing meant to outlive the party, while a bard's verses are built to carry a community's memory.
A storyteller stops short of a bard — the tales may hold a room, but a bard shapes them into verse and song and carries a whole people's memory in them.

A minstrel is a working entertainer who sings wherever there is supper and a crowd to please. A bard does more than entertain: a bard composes verse that keeps a community's memory. The minstrel plays for tonight's coins; the bard sings a people's story meant to last.

A troubadour is a courtly singer-poet devoted above all to polished songs of love. A bard's range is wider and weightier — history, grief, a town's whole life set into verse. A compliment sung beneath a castle window is troubadour work; a people's memory in song belongs to the bard.

Celtic bardos left no other everyday English word behind — bard is the root, whole and alone. When England crowned Shakespeare 'the Bard of Avon,' the old Celtic title had become the highest compliment poetry offers.
Bard means a poet, often a singer as well.

When the mine closed, a retired welder became the town's bard: he set the shutdown, the picket winter, and the last cage-lift down in rhyming stanzas and sang them at the union hall until everyone under thirty knew the story by heart.
Bard fits because a bard is a poet, often a singer as well — he did not just report what happened; he made it memory, composed in verse and carried aloud.
A narrator only tells a story; a bard composes it, keeps it, and sings a community's own life back to it.
Bard carries honor and age: use it for poets who sing a community's memory, or, capital-B, for Shakespeare.
This unit's narrator tells a story aloud without composing it; a minstrel entertains for pay.
Calling a modern songwriter a bard is pointed praise, not plain description.

The night the Greenbrier broke its banks in 1937, half of Marrow's Bend washed away.
What the town still holds of that night it owes to Ellis Vance, its bard: within a year he had set the flood into thirty verses, naming the lost families one by one.
He was not paid, and he refused to perform for touring strangers.
He taught the song to the schoolchildren, and they taught it to theirs.
Folklorists who arrived decades later expecting a quaint jingle found something else: a sung record, accurate enough to check against the county's own death rolls.
Ask anyone in Marrow's Bend who was lost in the flood, and they will not reach for a book.
